name: Rooftop, above the noise
desc: Someone climbed up here to send one message and wait for an answer.

shots.desc: the flat gravel roof of a city building at night ringed by chain link fence, cluttered with air conditioning units, ventilation ducts and a water tank, a skyline of lit windows standing below the parapet, every window and sign in frame a saturated coloured source, wide shot, no humans
one figure sitting on the roof parapet with back to the drop, the water tank and ducts behind, coloured city glow filling the whole background, full body, wide shot
a phone face-up on the gravel beside an air conditioning unit, its screen the brightest thing in frame, cables and duct runs around it, close-up, no humans
lit only from below by a phone screen, magenta and cyan from the city catching the other side of the jaw, eyes down on the screen, close-up
an aircraft warning light blinking on a mast above the roof, haze around it, the glow of the city underlighting low cloud, no humans

why: The rooftop is where a character goes to be reachable and alone at the same time, and this template is built on that contradiction: the whole city is visible and none of it is looking. The place card is emphatic that a default rooftop is an empty grey rectangle with a skyline pasted behind it, so every shot names the furniture - fence, ducts, water tank, warning mast - because the furniture is what makes it a place and gives a figure something to sit against. The parapet is named on the master specifically, because without it the roof runs off to nothing and the drop becomes invisible, and the drop is the reason anyone comes up here. The phone is given a whole insert of its own before the face that is lit by it, so the light source is established as a thing before it is used as a light - which is the only reliable way to get underlighting out of this model. The last beat is a warning light blinking to nobody, which is the same message the character just sent.
note: Not rendered. No frame from this template has been generated - the GPU was held for a video job - so everything below is read off the style, place and look cards rather than seen. Read the collision warning on the style card before changing the look. cyberpunk_neon's tags are almost verbatim the same words as studio/looks/neon.json - neon lights, night, city street, glowing sign, wet pavement, reflection - so setting look:neon here would spend the same tokens twice. look:night is used instead, and it is also the lowest saturation this style can safely take: cyberpunk_neon is chromatic by construction and any grade below 0.7 drains it, with night sitting at exactly 0.72. Do not drop to sodium at 0.65. Second thing the card is blunt about: this style does not darken the frame and never did - night, dark background moved mean luma 170 to 161, i.e. nothing. The dark is entirely the ffmpeg grade's job. Measured elsewhere and load-bearing here: on the qwen photographic path the thing that breaks in motion is the SHOT, not the texture. photorealistic and brutalist both held skin and concrete cleanly for four seconds and then lost the frame when the subject walked out of it (detail 0.964 at 4s against 0.510 at 8s). Be precise about what pace does and does not do about that, because it is easy to get wrong. pace does NOT change how much video is generated: compile.py leaves clip_secs at 6.0 on every beat, and clip_secs is not one of the sixteen keys the wizard accepts, so no template can set it. What pace changes is how much of that six seconds the EDIT shows - it writes intensity as 1/scale and scripts/scene_templates.py divides each cut length by it, so a fast beat shows roughly the first 1.3 to 2.9 seconds of the clip and a slow establish shows 5.7 of it. pace:normal and pace:fast keep the visible window inside the range that was measured to hold; pace:slow spends it. If drift still shows, lower clip_secs by hand in the .movie - do not reach for pace. Engine note: on qwen a face is held by a reference SHEET through Qwen-Edit rather than by IPAdapter, which is a weaker lock than the illustration path - expect visible drift between shots of the same person. Keep that in mind before casting one character across all of these beats. Applies to every card in this set and to none of the existing twenty: these templates use place CARDS rather than free text, so the place's own prose is appended to the prompt on top of whatever the shot desc says, and where a desc also names the setting the nouns arrive twice. That is reinforcement rather than contradiction, and it is deliberate on the shots whose place card warns that a particular noun must be named explicitly or the location renders wrong. But if a prompt reads long, the shot desc is the half to trim - never the card. Standing gaps that apply to every card in the gallery: transitions are intent only, because short.py hard-cuts every join regardless of what is set here; every emotion card is status:partial upstream, so the face, eyes, mouth and body tags render and voice_style does not, because no TTS engine on this box takes an emotion vector; and a style's negative_add never reaches the picture, because the renderer has no negative input wired - so this style will come out slightly less clean than its library sample, which had one.
